questions.prompt: An endocrine gland is triggered to send a chemical message to the rest of the body. What does it do?
options: Sends an electrical impulse down a nerve fiber
Releases a hormone into the bloodstream
Directly touches the target cell to pass the message
Absorbs the target cell's receptor into itself
questions.explanation: A gland is a hormone-producing organ. When triggered, it releases its hormone directly into nearby blood vessels, letting the bloodstream carry the chemical message throughout the body rather than sending it along a single wire-like path.
questions.misconception: Because both the nervous and endocrine systems send 'messages,' students sometimes assume every body signal travels along a nerve fiber. A gland has no nerve-fiber output for its hormone — it releases the hormone straight into the blood.

questions.prompt: A hormone released by the pancreas needs to reach muscle cells all over the body. How does it get there?
options: Through nerve cells relaying an electrical signal
By traveling through the bloodstream
By diffusing directly through the air inside the body
Through muscle contractions pushing it along
questions.explanation: Hormones are chemical messengers released into the blood. The heart continuously pumps blood everywhere, so a hormone made in one place, like the pancreas, can reach target cells anywhere in the body.
questions.misconception: It's easy to mix up hormone signaling with nerve signaling. Nerves do send fast electrical impulses along fixed cell fibers, but hormones take the slower, whole-body route through blood vessels instead of a dedicated wire-like pathway.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a hormone affect every single cell it passes on its trip through the bloodstream?
options: Hormones only flow to nearby cells, not far ones
Only cells with a matching receptor can respond to that hormone
Hormones dissolve before reaching most cells
Hormones only work while still inside the blood vessel
questions.explanation: Only cells that carry a receptor shaped to match the hormone can bind it and respond, like a lock that only opens for one specific key. Cells without that matching receptor let the hormone pass by with no effect.
questions.misconception: A common assumption is that traveling everywhere in the blood means affecting everything it touches. In reality, a hormone can flow right past a cell that simply doesn't have the matching receptor, so nothing happens there.

questions.prompt: A hormone has just bound to the receptor on a target cell's surface. What happens next?
options: Nothing more — binding alone is the entire response
The receptor triggers a chain of changes inside the cell, altering what the cell does
The target cell immediately releases its own hormone back into the bloodstream
The hormone is instantly destroyed and the cell returns to its resting state
questions.explanation: Binding is the trigger, not the finish line. Once a hormone binds its matching receptor, that sets off a chain of changes inside the cell — for example switching a gene on or speeding up an existing process — which is the actual response the hormone was 'asking for.'
questions.misconception: Learners often treat receptor binding as the endpoint of the story, missing that the real payoff — the cell doing something differently — happens after binding, inside the cell.

questions.prompt: After eating a meal, insulin helps lower your blood sugar. Once blood sugar returns to a healthy level, what typically happens next?
options: The pancreas keeps releasing insulin at the same steady rate forever
Feedback signals tell the pancreas to slow down or stop releasing insulin
The bloodstream stops carrying any hormones for the rest of the day
The target cells destroy the pancreas gland
questions.explanation: Most hormone pathways use negative feedback: once the response, like lowered blood sugar, reaches a healthy level, a signal loops back to the gland so it reduces hormone release. This keeps the body balanced instead of overcorrecting.
questions.misconception: Students often picture glands as releasing hormones at a constant, unchanging rate. Actually, feedback loops are constantly adjusting hormone release up or down based on what the body currently needs.

questions.prompt: Which statement best compares hormone signaling to nerve signaling?
options: Hormone signals are electrical while nerve signals are chemical
Hormone signals are typically slower to start but longer-lasting; nerve signals are typically fast but brief
They are exactly the same process, just using different organs
Hormone signals only affect bones while nerve signals only affect muscles
questions.explanation: Nerve signals are fast electrical impulses that trigger quick, short-lived responses, like yanking your hand off a hot stove. Hormone signals travel through the blood, so they take longer to arrive, but their effects, like growth or changes in metabolism, often last much longer.
questions.misconception: It's tempting to think faster is simply 'better,' or that the two systems do the same job. The body actually relies on nerves for split-second reactions and hormones for slower, sustained regulation — the two systems work together rather than compete.
